# Gallbladder and bile

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Basics of gastroenterology > Gallbladder and bile*

[Original Article Link](/library/Q60ukS)

---

## Summary

The <u>gallbladder</u> is an <u>intraperitoneal organ</u> derived from the <u>endoderm</u> that is located inferior to the <u>liver</u>. It is divided into a fundus, a body, often an infundibulum, and a neck. The <u>gallbladder</u> is <u>perfused</u> by the <u>cystic artery</u>, a branch of the <u>right hepatic artery</u> that drains into the <u>cystic vein</u> and the <u>hepatic sinusoids</u>. It receives <u>sympathetic</u> innervation via the <u>celiac plexus</u>, <u>parasympathetic</u> innervation via the <u>vagus nerve</u>, and sensory innervation via the branches of the <u>phrenic nerve</u>. The main function of the <u>gallbladder</u> is <u>bile</u> storage. <u>Bile</u> is secreted by the <u>liver</u> and facilitates digestion, neutralization of <u>gastric acid</u>, fat absorption, and excretion of <u>bilirubin</u> and <u>cholesterol</u>. The <u>biliary tract</u>, which is divided into intrahepatic and extrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts, transports <u>bile</u> to the intestine. The ductules are intrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts that unite to form the left and right hepatic ducts, which drain <u>bile</u> from the <u>liver</u>. The extrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts include the <u>cystic duct</u> and the <u>common hepatic duct</u>, which unite to form the <u>common bile duct</u>. The <u>common bile duct</u> unites with the <u>pancreatic duct</u> and drains into the <u>hepatopancreatic ampulla</u> in the <u>duodenum</u>. Excessive saturation of <u>bile</u> with <u>cholesterol</u> or <u>bilirubin</u> leads to <u>gallstone</u> formation. Diseases of the <u>biliary tract</u> include <u>cholecystitis</u>, <u>primary sclerosing cholangitis</u>, and biliary atresias among many others.

---

## Gallbladder

The <u>gallbladder</u> is a hollow, pear-like-shaped (piriform) organ that lies on the cystic plate (<u>gallbladder</u> bed) under the <u>liver</u> segments <u>IVB</u> and V. The cystic plate is a fibroareolar tissue that attaches the superior surface of the <u>gallbladder</u> to the <u>liver</u>.




### Anatomy




* Location: <u>intraperitoneal organ</u>

* Size and volume

* Length: 7–10 cm

* Width: 2.5 cm (at its widest point)

* Volume

* 30–35 mL under normal conditions

* Can hold up to 300 mL if the <u>cystic duct</u> is obstructed

* Composition/structure

* Fundus

* Body

* Infundibulum: the section that narrows from the body to the neck

* Sometimes described in literature as part of the neck

* Inaccurately described in some literature as synonymous with the Hartmann Pouch

* Neck: connects to the <u>cystic duct</u> → <u>common hepatic duct</u> → <u>common bile duct</u>

* Possible Hartmann gallbladder pouch

* A dilation that may be seen on the <u>ventral</u> aspect of the <u>gallbladder</u>, <u>proximal</u> to the <u>gallbladder</u> neck

* Most common site of <u>gallstone</u> impaction

* Previously thought to be a pathologic finding but now thought to be an anatomic variant





![Extrahepatic biliary tree](media/hz8zo26cawx1s229cfzp0hev.jpg)

Extrahepatic biliary tree




### Function




* Storage of <u>bile</u>

* <u>Bile</u> drains from the <u>liver</u> via small <u>bile</u> ducts.

* <u>Cholecystokinin</u> (<u>CCK</u>) stimulates the <u>gallbladder</u> to contract, which then releases <u>bile</u> through the <u>cystic duct</u>, into the <u>second part of the duodenum</u>.

* Concentration of <u>bile</u>: by absorption of <u>electrolytes</u> and water





### Vasculature




* Arterial blood supply: cystic artery (branch of the <u>right hepatic artery</u>)

* Venous drainage

* Neck: <u>cystic veins</u> → <u>portal vein</u>

* Body and fundus: <u>hepatic sinusoids</u>





### Innervation




* <u>Sympathetic</u>: via the <u>celiac plexus</u>

* <u>Parasympathetic</u>: hepatic branch of the <u>vagus nerve</u>

* Sensory: fibers from the <u>phrenic nerve</u> → <u>referred pain</u> to the right shoulder area (via C3 nerve fibers)





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Cholecystitis</u> causes <u>referred pain</u> to the right shoulder region because the <u>phrenic nerve</u> originates from <u>spinal nerves</u> C3–C5, which also provide somatic sensation to the shoulder area.

## Biliary tract

### Anatomy




The biliary tree is divided into the intrahepatic and extrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts.




#### Intrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts




* Bile canaliculi → intrahepatic bile ductules (<u>canals of Hering</u>) → segmental <u>bile</u> ducts → sectional ducts

* Right <u>posterior</u> duct (RPD): drains segment VI and VII

* Right <u>anterior</u> duct (<u>RAD</u>): drains segment V and VIII

* Right <u>posterior</u> and <u>anterior</u> ducts connect and form the right hepatic duct (<u>RHD</u>).

* <u>Bile</u> ducts from segments II–IV connect and form the left hepatic duct (LHD).

* Common hepatic duct (<u>CHD</u>): formed by the right and left hepatic ducts





#### Extrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts




* Common bile duct 

* Formed by the <u>common hepatic duct</u> and cystic duct

* Travels in the free edge of the <u>lesser omentum</u>, in the <u>hepatoduodenal ligament</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> to the <u>duodenum</u> and the <u>pancreas</u>

* Connects with the <u>main pancreatic duct</u>

* Drains into the hepatopancreatic ampulla (<u>ampulla of Vater</u>)

* Hepatobiliary triangle

* An anatomical space formed by the <u>common hepatic duct</u>, the <u>cystic duct</u>, and the inferior border of the <u>liver</u>

* Contains the <u>cystic artery</u> and the cystic <u>lymph node</u> (Lund's node)

* During <u>cholecystectomy</u>, the <u>hepatobiliary triangle</u> must be carefully identified to prevent damage to the <u>cystic artery</u> and extrahepatic <u>biliary system</u>.

* Calot triangle: an anatomical space formed by the <u>common hepatic duct</u>, the <u>cystic duct</u>, and the <u>cystic artery</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>portal triad</u> consists of the hepatic <u>artery</u>, <u>portal vein</u>, and <u>common bile duct</u>.

## Bile

### Composition




<u>Bile</u> is a secretion produced by the <u>liver</u> and stored in the <u>gallbladder</u> that aids in digestion, neutralization of <u>gastric acid</u>, fat absorption, and excretion of <u>bilirubin</u> and <u>cholesterol</u>.




* Bile pigments

* <u>Bilirubin</u> (yellow pigment)

* Excreted as water-soluble (conjugated) <u>bilirubin</u>

* Conjugated within the <u>liver</u>

* Transported in the blood bound to carrier <u>proteins</u>

* Lipid soluble (unconjugated) metabolite of <u>hemoglobin</u>

* <u>Biliverdin</u> (green pigment): a byproduct of <u>hemoglobin breakdown</u>

* Bile acids

* <u>Primary bile acids</u>

* Cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid

* Synthesized in the <u>liver</u> from <u>cholesterol</u> (rate-limiting enzyme: cholesterol 7-α hydroxylase)

* Stored in the <u>gallbladder</u>

* <u>Secondary bile acids</u>

* Deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid

* Synthesized in the intestinal lumen by the action of bacterial flora

* <u>Bile acids</u> are conjugated with <u>glycine</u> or taurine to form bile salts and become water-soluble.

* Other components: phospholipids, <u>cholesterol</u>, water, and ions





> [!NOTE]
> A deficiency of <u>bile acids</u> can result in fat <u>malabsorption</u> and <u>cholesterol stones</u> in the <u>gallbladder</u>.




![Bilirubin](media/zb8bg7oezxayvxv5apdsibcd.jpg)

Bilirubin

![Cholic acid](media/c7lwovz99vhsiadadavsv8b0.jpg)

Cholic acid

![Glycocholic acid](media/r2t4j577nhr3lwis78yx0bhk.jpg)

Glycocholic acid

![Taurocholic acid](media/ydna8vwy6ctt6mim0er2sw4h.jpg)

Taurocholic acid




### Function




* Emulsion and absorption of fats (including <u>fat-soluble vitamins</u>)

* Excretion of <u>bilirubin</u> and <u>cholesterol</u> (the process by which the majority of <u>cholesterol</u> is removed from the body)

* Antimicrobial effect (may disrupt bacterial membranes)

* Transport of <u>IgA</u>





### Enterohepatic circulation




Substances metabolized in the <u>liver</u> are excreted into the <u>bile</u>.




* <u>Bile salts</u> (∼ 95% of <u>bile acids</u> are reabsorbed back into the <u>liver</u> to be recycled)

* Pass into the intestinal lumen where bacteria break down <u>primary bile acids</u> into <u>secondary bile acids</u>

* Get reabsorbed in the intestinal <u>mucosa</u> (primarily the <u>proximal</u> and <u>distal</u> <u>ileum</u>)

* Return to the <u>liver</u> via portal circulation

* <u>Bilirubin</u> 

* ∼ 80% is excreted in feces as <u>stercobilin</u> .

* ∼ 20% enters <u>enterohepatic circulation</u>.

* ∼ 90% is recycled in the <u>liver</u>.

* ∼ 10% is excreted by the <u>kidney</u>.





![Bilirubin metabolism](media/utmsqnzocugk58qh9nsw8vzr.jpg)

Bilirubin metabolism




### Gallstones




There are different types of <u>gallstones</u> (see “<u>Cholelithiasis</u>” and “<u>Cholecystitis</u>” for more information):




* Cholesterol stones (∼ 80% of cases)

* <u>Radiolucent</u> with <u>radiopaque</u> areas due to calcifications (< 20%)

* Composed of <u>cholesterol</u> and <u>calcium carbonate</u>

* Pigment gallstones

* Black pigment gallstones

* <u>Radiopaque</u>

* Associated with <u>hemolytic</u> diseases such as <u>sickle cell anemia</u>, <u>hereditary spherocytosis</u>

* Composed of <u>calcium</u> bilirubinate

* Brown pigment gallstones

* <u>Radiolucent</u>

* Associated with infection





![Pathophysiology for different types of gallstones](media/j6cdxxxdr8u1ay9a6zwsgez4.jpg)

Pathophysiology for different types of gallstones

## Clinical significance

### Disorders of the biliary tract




* <u>Primary sclerosing cholangitis</u>

* <u>Primary biliary cholangitis</u>

* <u>Ascending cholangitis</u>

* <u>Choledocholithiasis</u>

* <u>Cholecystitis</u>

* <u>Porcelain gallbladder</u>

* <u>Biliary colic</u>

* <u>Cholelithiasis</u>

* <u>Gallbladder polyp</u>

* <u>Cholangiocarcinoma</u>

* <u>Mirizzi syndrome</u>

* <u>Biliary atresia</u>

* <u>Choledochal cyst</u>

* <u>Caroli disease</u>

* Cholesterolosis (<u>cholesterol</u> deposits within <u>macrophages</u>, which causes a yellowish, speckled <u>mucosal</u> coloration due to excess <u>cholesterol</u> in <u>bile</u>)





### Disorders of the bile




* <u>Neonatal jaundice</u>

* <u>Crohn disease</u>

* <u>Primary bile acid</u> <u>diarrhea</u>

* <u>Small intestine bacterial overgrowth</u>

* <u>Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy</u>

* <u>Celiac disease</u>

* <u>Chronic pancreatitis</u>

* <u>Gilbert syndrome</u>

* <u>Crigler-Najjar syndrome</u>

* <u>Dubin-Johnson syndrome</u>

* <u>Rotor syndrome</u>

* <u>Primary bile acid</u> <u>malabsorption</u> (PBAM)





### Disorders of the intestine




* <u>Short bowel syndrome</u>

* <u>Crohn disease</u>
